en: In the *Wanling Lu* (Record of Wanling) of Chan Master Huangbo Duanjì, Minister Pei asked the Master:
"Among the four or five hundred people in the mountains, how many have attained the Dharma of the Master? The Master replied:
"Those who have attained it cannot be measured by number. Why? Because the Way is realized through the mind; how could it [be measured] otherwise?"
These are spoken words;
such speech is merely for the purpose of transforming the ignorant.
[The question: "What is the Buddha?"
The Master said:
"The very mind is Buddha;
the absence of mind is the Way."
It is simply that one must not give rise to thoughts or mental stirrings concerning existence and non-existence, long and short, self and other, subject and object, and so forth.
The mind is fundamentally the Buddha;
the Buddha is fundamentally the mind.
The mind is like empty space.
Thus it is said:
"The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space."
Do not seek elsewhere;
all seeking is suffering.
Even if one were to practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.
Nor is it ultimate.
Why? Because it belongs to that which is produced through causes and conditions.
When causes and conditions are exhausted, one returns to impermanence.
Therefore it is said:
"The retributive and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha."
Nor is it one who preaches the Dharma.
It is simply the recognition of one's own mind:
being without self and without person, it is fundamentally Buddha.
Question: "If the sage’s state of no-mind is itself Buddhahood, does the ordinary person’s state of no-mind not lead to sinking into emptiness and stillness?
The Master said:
In the Dharma, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor is there stillness or silence.
The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent;
do not fall into the view of nihilism.
The Dharma is fundamentally not non-existent;
do not form views of existence.
Both existence and non-existence are merely views born of the deluded mind.
It is like a magical illusion or a cataract.
Thus it is said:
"Seeing and hearing are like a magical illusion or a cataract."
Discriminative cognition belongs to sentient beings;
within the school of the Patriarchs, one speaks only of ceasing mental activity and forgetting views.
Therefore, when mental activity is forgotten, the Buddha-way flourishes.
When there is conceptual discrimination, the armies of Māra flourish.
Question: Since the mind is fundamentally the Buddha, does one still cultivate the six pāramitās and the myriad practices?
The Master said:
"Awakening resides within the mind;
it is not contingent upon the six perfections or the myriad practices."
The six perfections and the myriad practices are all merely gateways of transformation for the peripheral task of engaging with sentient beings and delivering them across the realms of rebirth.
Even such things as bodhi, true thusness, the limit of reality, liberation, and the dharma-body—
extending even to the noble stages of the ten bhūmis and the four fruits— are likewise so.
All these are gateways to liberation;
they do not concern the Buddha-mind.
The mind itself is the Buddha.
Therefore, among all the gateways of the perfections (*pāramitā*), the Buddha-mind is foremost.
It is simply that when there is no mind of birth-and-death or afflictions (*kleśa*),
one does not employ dharmas such as bodhi.
Therefore it is said:
"The Buddha taught all dharmas to deliver my entire mind."
I have no mind at all;
what use have I for all dharmas?
From the Buddha down to the Patriarchs.
It does not discuss other matters,
but discusses only the one mind;
it is also called the One Vehicle.
Therefore, when sought thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle;
this assembly has no branches or leaves,
consisting only of those who are steadfast and true.
For this reason, this meaning is difficult to believe.
Since the arrival of Dharma in this land,
it has reached the two kingdoms of Liang and Wei.
There was only Master Ke,
who secretly trusted his own mind and attained realization the moment he heard the words.
The very mind is Buddha;
when both body and mind are absent,
this is called the Great Way.
The Great Way is fundamentally equal; therefore,
one has deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature,
and that the nature of the mind is no different.
Nature is identical to mind;
mind does not differ from nature.
This is what is called the Patriarch.
Therefore it is said:
"When one recognizes the mind-nature,
it may be called inconceivable."
Question: "Does the Buddha deliver sentient beings?
The Master said:
"In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers."
Since even a self cannot be apprehended,
how could that which is not-self be apprehended?
Both the Buddha and sentient beings are likewise unapprehendable.
[The student] said: "You speak of manifesting the thirty-two marks and delivering sentient beings;
how can you say they do not exist? The Master said:
All marks whatsoever are empty and false.
If one perceives all marks as non-marks,
then one sees the Tathāgata.
Both the Buddhas and sentient beings are entirely the products of your deluded vision;
it is simply because you do not recognize your original mind that you vainly construct such views.
As soon as one forms the view of seeing a Buddha, one is obstructed by the Buddha;
as soon as one forms the view of seeing a sentient being, one is obstructed by sentient beings;
and so it is with views of ordinary or holy, pure or defiled, and so forth.
They all become obstacles.
Because they obstruct your mind, they collectively result in saṃsāra,
just as a monkey that lets go of one thing only to seize another never finds a moment of rest.
First is learning;
one must simply be beyond learning.
There is neither ordinary person nor sage.
Neither pure nor defiled;
neither great nor small;
without outflows and unconditioned.
In this single mind,
through skillful means and diligent adornment,
you shall listen to and master the twelvefold teachings of the Three Vehicles.
All views must be completely relinquished.
Therefore, having removed everything,
he placed only a single bed and lay there ill.
It is simply this: not giving rise to any views,
there is not a single dharma to be apprehended,
and one is not obstructed by dharmas.
Having transcended the realms of both ordinary beings and sages within the three worlds,
one may for the first time be named a world-transcending Buddha.
Therefore it is said:
I prostrate to the one who is like space, having no dependence and transcending all non-Buddhists;
since the mind is not different,
the Dharma is likewise not different.
Since the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), phenomena (*dharma*) are also unconditioned.
All phenomena arise entirely through the transformations of the mind;
therefore, because my mind is empty, all phenomena are empty.
The thousands of grades and myriad species are all identical.
Throughout the entirety of the empty realms of the ten directions, there is but the single substance of mind.
Mind is fundamentally not different from phenomena, and phenomena are likewise not different from mind.
It is simply because your views and understandings differ that there is such a distinction.
It is like when the various devas eat from the same precious vessel; according to their respective merits, the color of the food appears different to each.
The Buddhas of the ten directions truly have not the slightest dharma that can be obtained,
which is what is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is simply the one mind, truly without any marks of difference.
It is likewise devoid of radiance and devoid of victory or defeat;
because there is no victory, there is no mark of a Buddha.
Because there is no attachment, there is no mark of a sentient being.
[The interlocutor asks:
"If the mind has no marks, how can it be that it entirely lacks the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics used to transform and deliver sentient beings?"
The Master said:
"The thirty-two marks belong to the realm of characteristics;
whatever has characteristics is entirely illusory."
The eighty secondary marks belong to form.
If one perceives me by means of form,
such a person walks in a perverted path.
They were unable to see the Tathāgata.
They then asked whether the Buddha-nature and the nature of sentient beings are identical or distinct.
The Master said:
"In its essential nature, there is neither sameness nor difference.
However, if we speak according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles,"
Thus, it is said that there is the Buddha-nature and the sentient-being-nature;
consequently, there are the causes and effects of the three vehicles,
and therein lies both similarity and difference.
If one refers to the Buddha Vehicle and the oral transmission of the patriarchs,
such matters are not spoken of;
there is only the single mind.
Neither identical nor different;
neither cause nor effect.
Therefore it is said: "There is only this One Vehicle path."
There is neither two nor three,
except for the Buddha’s skillful means of teaching.
Question:
"Why does the Bodhisattva Anantagātra not see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown?
The Master said:
In reality, there is nothing to be seen. Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva Boundless Body is himself the Tathāgata.
One should not see anything further.
I am merely teaching you not to form the view of a Buddha, so as not to fall into the extreme of Buddhahood;
and not to form the view of a sentient being, so as not to fall into the extreme of sentient beings.
One does not form the view of existence nor fall into the extreme of existence;
one does not form the view of non-existence nor fall into the extreme of non-existence;
one does not form the view of the ordinary nor fall into the extreme of the ordinary.
Not forming holy views and not falling into the extremes of holiness—
merely being without any views is itself the boundless body (*anantakāya*).
If there is a place for views, one is called a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
Followers of external paths delight in various views,
whereas a bodhisattva remains unmoved by all views.
A Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
Therefore it is said:
"The infinite is also suchness;
all sages and worthies are also suchness."
Suchness is non-arising;
suchness is non-ceasing;
suchness is non-seeing.
As it is, there is no hearing.
The Tathāgata’s crown is itself perfect vision;
because there is also no perfect vision, one does not fall into the extreme of perfection.
Therefore, the Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories;
it uses empty space as a metaphor because it is perfectly identical to the great void, lacking nothing and having no remainder.
When there is nothing to do in the ordinary state, do not forcibly discriminate other realms.
Once you engage in discrimination, it immediately becomes consciousness.
Therefore, it is said:
The perfected nature sinks into the ocean of consciousness;
its cyclic flow is like a drifting tumbleweed.
One merely says, "I know," "I have learned," "I have attained realization," "I am liberated," or "I possess the Way."
What use is such a view as this,
which holds that what is strong is as one wishes while what is weak is contrary to one's wishes?
I tell you: when there is nothing to do in the ordinary course of life, do not waste your effort;
there is no need to seek the Truth.
One need only cease [false] views.
For this reason, both internal and external views are erroneous;
both the path of the Buddha and the path of Māra are equally evil.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī briefly gave rise to two views and was banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains;
yet Mañjuśrī is, in truth, ultimate wisdom.
Samantabhadra is expedient wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
Although expedient means and reality are contrasted as antidotes, ultimately there is neither expedient means nor reality;
it is solely the one mind.
When the mind is neither Buddha nor sentient being, there is no divergent view.
As soon as there is the view of a Buddha, there arises the view of a sentient being;
thus there arise views of existence and non-existence, and views of permanence and annihilation.
Thus, the two Iron Ring Mountains are formed;
because they are obstructed by what is seen,
the Patriarch directly pointed to the original mind of all sentient beings.
The fundamental essence is inherently Buddha;
it is not produced through cultivation and does not belong to gradual stages.
It is neither light nor darkness.
Because it is not light, there is no light;
because it is not darkness, there is no darkness.
Therefore, there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance.
Those who enter this gate of my school must take care to keep this in mind.
Seeing is called "Dharma";
seeing the Dharma is called "Buddha.
Both Buddha and Dharma are non-existent.
This is called the Sangha;
it is termed the Unconditioned Sangha,
and is also named the Single-Entity Triple Gem.
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha,
nor does he seek by clinging to the Dharma.
One does not cling to seeking among the multitude;
one should be without anything to seek.
Because one does not cling to seeking for a Buddha, there is no Buddha.
Because there is no seeking through attachment to dharmas, there is no Dharma;
because there is no seeking through attachment to the assembly, there is no Sangha.
Question:
"The Master is currently preaching the Dharma;
how can you say that there is neither Sangha nor Dharma?
The Teacher replied:
If you perceive any dharma that can be spoken of,
you are seeking me by means of sound.
If you perceive a self, that is a locus.
Dharmas are also non-dharmas;
dharmas are precisely the mind.
Therefore, the Patriarch said:
When transmitting this mind-dharma,
how could dharma ever be dharma?
There is no dharma and no fundamental mind.
One first understands that both mind and mental factors are ultimately such that not a single dharma can be said to "sit at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
The site of enlightenment is simply the non-arising of all views.
To realize that all phenomena are fundamentally empty is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Originally, there has not been a single thing.
Where is there any dust?
If one grasps the meaning within this,
what need is there to discuss wandering at ease?
Question:
"From the very beginning there has not been a single thing.
Does this mean that 'no-thing' is precisely what it is?
The Master said:
"Even 'non-existence' is not it;
for there is no place where Bodhi exists."
Nor is there any lack of understanding.
Question:
What is the Buddha?
The Master said:
"Your mind is the Buddha;
the Buddha is your mind."
The mind and the Buddha are not different;
therefore, it is said that "the mind itself is the Buddha.
Apart from the mind, there is no other Buddha.
[The student] asked: "If one's own mind is the Buddha, how did the Patriarch transmit the teaching when he came from the West?
The Master said:
The Patriarch came from the West solely to transmit the Buddha-mind,
directly pointing out that your own mind is fundamentally the Buddha.
Because mind after mind is no different, he is called the Patriarch.
If one directly perceives this meaning,
one immediately transcends all stages of the three vehicles;
one is originally a Buddha, not requiring cultivation or achievement.
[The student] said, "If this is so,
what Dharma do the Buddhas of the ten directions teach when they appear in the world?
The Master said:
The Buddhas of the ten directions appearing in the world all together preach only the Dharma of the One Mind;
this is why the Buddha secretly entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa.
This essence of the single dharma of mind pervades all of space and permeates the entire dharma-realm;
it is called the theoretical principle of all Buddhas.
How could this Dharma be understood by you through words and phrases?
Nor can it be seen within a single stimulus or a single object.
This meaning can only be realized through silent, intuitive penetration.
This gate is named the Gate of Unconditioned Dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If one wishes to realize it, one need only know the state of no-mind;
upon sudden awakening, one immediately attains it.
If you apply the mind with the intent to learn and grasp it,
it will immediately move further away.
If there is no bifurcated mind and no mind of grasping or rejecting, [it is attained].
When the mind is like wood or stone,
one first possesses the capacity to study the Way.
It is said that at present there exist various kinds of deluded thoughts.
"Why do you say it does not exist?
The Master replied,
"Delusion fundamentally has no substance."
This is precisely what has arisen from your own mind.
If you recognize that the mind is the Buddha,
then the mind is fundamentally without delusion.
How could you give rise to a mind that further identifies with delusion?
If you do not produce thoughts or stir your mind,
there will naturally be no delusion.
Therefore it is said:
"When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease."
[The student] asked, "Right now, at the very moment a deluded thought arises,
where is the Buddha?
The Master said:
When you now perceive the arising of delusion,
that very perception is the Buddha.
If within this there were no delusion, the Buddha would also not exist.
Why is this so? Because you give rise to the thought of becoming a Buddha,
you then claim that there is a Buddha to be accomplished.
To give rise to the view of sentient beings is to claim that there are sentient beings who can be saved;
every stirring of thought and movement of mind is entirely your own point of view.
If there were no view of anything at all,
where would the Buddha be? For instance,
as soon as Mañjuśrī gave rise to the view of a Buddha, he was banished to between the two Iron Ring Mountains.
[The student] asked: "At this very moment of awakening, where is the Buddha?
The Master said:
Question: From where do they come?
From what do awakening arise?
And as for all sounds and forms—speaking and silence, movement and stillness?
All is Buddha-work;
where can one seek the Buddha?
One must not further place a head upon a head or add a beak to a beak.
Simply do not give rise to divergent views.
The mountain is the mountain and the water is the water;
the monastics are monastics and the laity are the laity.
The mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars—
all do not transcend your mind.
The entire trichiliocosm is, in its entirety, your very own self.
Where is there so much variety?
Outside the mind there is no dharma; before one's eyes are green mountains.
The world of empty space is brilliantly clear.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of this that you may take as a conceptual view.
Therefore, all sounds and forms are the Buddha’s eye of wisdom.
Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they are produced only by relying upon their objects.
For the sake of things, one possesses manifold wisdom;
yet throughout the entire day one speaks, what has ever been spoken?
Throughout the entire day one hears, what has ever been heard?
Therefore, although Śākyamuni preached for forty-nine years,
he never spoke a single word.
If it is as you say, then...
"Where is Bodhi?
The Master said,
"Bodhi has no such place."
The Buddha does not attain bodhi,
nor do sentient beings lose bodhi;
it cannot be attained by means of the body.
One cannot seek it with the mind.
Since all sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi,
how can one give rise to the bodhicitta?
The Master said:
"Bodhi is unattainable.
You should now simply give rise to a mind that is itself unattainable."
One definitively does not apprehend a single dharma;
this is precisely the bodhicitta.
Bodhi has no place of abiding.
Therefore, there is no one who attains.
Thus it is said:
"In the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I did not obtain even the slightest dharma."
The Buddha then bestowed upon me a prediction:
"One clearly knows that all sentient beings are fundamentally bodhi;
they need not further attain bodhi."
Now that you have heard the arousal of the bodhicitta,
you may think that by learning this single mind you will become a Buddha;
you intend only to become a Buddha.
Even if you were to practice for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
you would only attain a Reward Buddha or an Emanation Buddha;
what connection would that have with the Buddha of your original source, true nature?
Therefore it is said:
"Seeking an external Buddha with form is not like you."
Question:
Since the fundamental nature is already Buddha,
why is there no longer the manifold variety of forms and appearances within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence?
The Master said:
"The essence of all Buddhas is perfect and complete, with neither increase nor decrease;
it flows into the six realms of existence, yet it is perfectly complete in every place."
Among the myriad species, each and every one is a Buddha.
It is like a mass of mercury scattered in various places;
every single drop is perfectly round.
If not divided, it is but a single block; this one is all,
and all is this one.
Various forms and appearances are like houses;
one abandons the house of an ass to enter the house of a human,
and abandons the human body to attain the celestial body.
Even the dwellings of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas,
and buddhas are all places where you engage in grasping and rejecting;
therefore, there exists a distinct nature of the original source.
How could there be any distinction?
Question:
How do the Buddhas practice great compassion?
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
The Master said:
"The compassion of the Buddha is without conditions."
Therefore, it is called Great Compassion.
"Compassion" (maitrī) means not perceiving that there is a Buddha to be realized;
"compassion" (karuṇā) means not perceiving that there are sentient beings to be delivered.
The Dharma he preaches is without preaching and without demonstration;
those who listen to the Dharma have neither hearing nor attainment.
It is like a phantom person preaching the Dharma for a phantom person.
If this Dharma were something to be attained through the Way, I would have grasped it from the words of my spiritual friend;
I have realized it and awakened to this very compassion.
If it were something you could acquire by stirring the mind and giving rise to thoughts to learn another's intellectual understanding, [it would not be so].
If one does not awaken to one's own fundamental mind,
it will ultimately be of no benefit.
Question:
"What is diligence?
The Master said,
"Neither body nor mind arises."
This is called the first form of firm and powerful diligence.
To merely give rise to the thought of seeking outwardly is said to be King Kali departing for his pleasure hunt.
When the mind does not wander outward,
this is precisely the patience of the Rishi; when both body and mind are non-existent,
this is precisely the Buddha-way.
Question:
"If one practices this path without mental activity, will it be attained?
The Master said:
To be without mind is precisely to practice this Way.
What more need be said of "attaining" or "not attaining"?
For instance, the mere flickering of a single thought is itself an object.
If there is not even a single thought, then the objective realm is forgotten and the mind naturally ceases;
there is nothing further to be pursued.
Question:
"What is it like to transcend the three realms?
The Master said,
"Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all."
At that very moment, one emerges from the three realms.
The Tathāgata appears in the world to destroy the three existences (trai-bhava).
If there is no mind whatsoever, [one transcends them].
The three realms are likewise non-existent;
it is like a single mote of dust broken into one hundred parts,
where ninety-nine of those parts are non-existent.
If there were even one part that existed,
the Mahāyāna would not be able to excel;
since it is entirely non-existent in a hundred parts, [it excels].
Only then can the Mahāyāna truly excel.
Ascending the hall, he said:
"The very mind is Buddha."
From the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects and sentient beings,
all possess Buddha-nature.
It is the same single mind-essence.
This is why Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven;
he transmitted nothing but the Dharma of the One Mind.
Directly pointing out that all sentient beings are originally Buddhas,
without depending on cultivation;
one need only now recognize one's own mind and perceive one's own original nature.
Do not seek anything else.
How does one recognize one's own mind?
That which is speaking these very words right now is precisely your own mind.
If it neither speaks nor engages in mental activity,
its essence is like empty space:
it has no characteristics and no location.
Nor is it exclusively non-existent and invisible.
Thus the Patriarch said:
"The true nature is the treasury of the mind-ground."
It has neither head nor tail;
it transforms sentient beings in accordance with conditions.
When it employs skillful means, it is called "wisdom"; when it does not respond to conditions, [it is otherwise].
It cannot be said to exist or not to exist;
even when it manifests in accordance with the proper occasion,
it leaves no trace.
Since you know this to be so,
simply dwelling now within the state of non-existence is itself walking the path of all Buddhas.
The Sūtra says:
"One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.
As for all sentient beings who transmigrate through birth and death:
The mind, driven by conditions,
wanders through the six realms of existence without ceasing,
thereby causing one to undergo various kinds of suffering.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The minds of those who are difficult to transform are like monkeys;
therefore, one restrains their minds through various kinds of dharmas."
Thereupon, they are subdued.
Thus, when the mind arises, various phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease.
Therefore, know that all dharmas are created by the mind.
Even humans, devas, earth-dwellers, hell-beings, the six realms, and asuras—
all are created by the mind.
Now, simply learn to be mindless and suddenly bring all conditions to rest.
Do not give rise to deluded thoughts or discrimination.
There is no person and no self.
Without greed or anger, without hatred or love, and without competition or victory;
merely by eliminating these various kinds of false imaginings,
one's nature is inherently pure from the very beginning.
This refers to those who practice the Dharma of Bodhi, such as the Buddhas and others.
If one does not comprehend this meaning,
then even if one studies extensively and practices with diligent effort, it will be in vain.
Those who eat wood and wear grass,
yet do not recognize their own minds, are all termed practitioners of deviant conduct;
they become entirely celestial demons, non-Buddhist heretics, and various deities of the waters and lands.
"If one practices in this manner,
what further benefit will there be?
Master Zhizhi said:
The fundamental substance is created by one's own mind;
how could it be sought within words?
Now, simply recognize your own mind.
Cease contemplation;
then delusive thoughts and the dust of worldly toil will naturally not arise.
As the Vimalakīrti-sūtra says:
He left only a single bed upon which he lay ill;
his mind did not arise [from its state of concentration],
remaining as he now lies prostrate with illness.
When all objects of perception have ceased and deluded thoughts have been extinguished,
this is itself bodhi.
If, at this moment, your mind is restless and unsettled,
then even if you study until you have attained the three vehicles, the four fruits, or the various stages of the ten bhūmis,
in the end you will merely remain seated among the ordinary and the holy.
All conditioned phenomena ultimately revert to impermanence;
their power and influence all have a limit.
They are like an arrow shot into the sky.
When their strength is exhausted,
they fall back once more into the cycle of birth and death;
such practitioners do not understand the Buddha’s intent.
To undergo suffering and hardship in vain—
is this not a great error?
Master Zhigong said:
Having not yet encountered a world-transcending enlightened teacher,
you have mistakenly donned the dharma-medicine of the Mahāyāna.
Now, at all times— whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— you should simply practice non-mind.
There is neither conceptual discrimination nor dependence;
there is neither dwelling nor attachment.
Throughout the day, one proceeds spontaneously and carefree.
"You are like a foolish person;
the people of the world do not recognize you at all.
Furthermore, you have no need to teach others whether they recognize you or not."
The mind is like a hard stone, entirely without seams or fissures;
no phenomena can penetrate into your mind.
It stands solitary and unattached.
Only then does there arise a slight degree of correspondence.
To penetrate beyond the realms of the three worlds is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
to be free from the characteristics of the mind is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
One does not perform the karma of humans or devas;
one does not perform the karma of hell-beings;
one does not give rise to any mental activity whatsoever.
When all conditions are exhausted, there is no arising;
this very body and mind are then a person of freedom.
This does not mean that there is an absolute non-arising.
It simply arises according to one's will.
As the Sūtra says:
"The Bodhisattva has a mind-born body (manomayakāya). This is precisely it.
If one suddenly fails to realize mindlessness and instead acts while attached to signs,
all such actions belong to the realm of demonic activity.
Even performing the Buddha-work of purifying the buddha-field constitutes an obstacle to Buddhahood;
all such activities are termed "obstacles to Buddhahood."
Because it obstructs your mind,
you are bound by cause and effect,
leaving you with no freedom of movement or stillness.
Therefore, dharmas such as bodhi are fundamentally non-existent;
this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
All these are emanated persons, just like yellow leaves used as gold to temporarily stop a child’s crying.
Therefore, in reality, there is no dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now that you have understood this meaning.
What is the use of such petty efforts?
Simply follow conditions to exhaust past karma,
and do not create further new calamities.
It is clear within the mind;
therefore, all former understandings must be relinquished.
